text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
- Elderly drivers will have their licences reviewed under new Swedish regulations.

- Business leader Leif Johansson is currently head of two major companies, AB Volvo and Electrolux, with a six day overlap as he moves jobs. It is the first time the same person had led two of Sweden's largest companies at the same time. Johansson, 46, said it was a technicality and meant little. He is leaving Electrolux to head Volvo, replacing Soren Gyll.

- Swedish-Swiss engineer ABB posted a pre-tax profit for the first three months of 1997 of $391 million which was 5.6 percent higher than in the first quarter of 1996. The stronger dollar had a negative effect on earnings.

- Shares in drugs company Astra continued to fall on the Stockholm bourse on Tuesday, dominating trade, after posting a weaker-than-expepcted first quarter report on Monday. Dealers said the fall was overdone.

- A survey by Sweden's Gallup found a group of key people for the future who are young and well-educated and do not feel particularly attached to Sweden. This is using an international method. About seven percent of youngsters will be key people and most of these are found in the big cities. Most are male.

- Drugs company Astra continues to tumble on the Stockholm bourse after posting its first quarter results, with a telephone conference with analysts failing to stop the fall. Some analysts have lowered their trading recommendations on the stock. Bear Sterns has lowered its from attractive to buy and Smith Barney from outperform to neutral.
- Engineer ABB posted a better result for the first quarter than expected and its share price rose.

- Despite opposition from Prime Minister Goran Persson, Swedish telecom operator Telia could be listed on the Stockholm Stock Exchange as early as spring 1999. Ines Uusman, communications minister, says that she no longer sees any ideological barriers to privatising the state-owned group.

- Strict costs controls sustained earnings for ABB, the Swedish-Swiss engineering conglomerate, during the first three months of 1997. Earnings rose six percent to $391 million despite a drop in sales. The Swedish company ABB AB's shares of profit after tax was 861 million crowns or 0.92 crowns a share diluted for the recent 10 to one split.

- A seat on the board of directors of a publicly traded company is won through long and loyal service rather than deep knowledge of the industry. At least that is one of the conclusions of a survey by the executive search consultancy Heidrick & Struggles presented at a seminar arranged by the firm and Rune Brandinger, current board member for Sandvik, Nordbanken and Wasakronan.
